Theoretical Quantum information research often leads to highly technical mathematical questions (e.g. see here). There are a number of collections out there, e.g. Werner's List, a community list hosted by IQOQI. Would you be interested in these sort of problems too?

I am sure there are more, and would be quite easy collecting them by asking the right people (one sees in many theoretical quantum papers open math questions in the discussions).

The effort of #Quantum information might be quite helpful in some of the formalisations (see the quantum info Lean github, which will be combined with PhysLean into PhysLib soon).

Let me know, i would be happy collecting more of them, and at least adding them as issues at github. In that case, let me know whether there is any procedure doing so, or can i just go ahead as with my previous issue?
Feel free to open new issues! (and the way you opened your first issue looks good!)
Great, i started with the first 5. There are 49 of them in general. Would it make sense to give a dedicated label for questions of this collection?
Does it make most sense to only make issues for open problems of the list, ignoring solved problems for now? @Moritz Firsching

Franz Huschenbeth said:

Does it make most sense to only make issues for open problems of the list, ignoring solved problems for now? Moritz Firsching

I would be fine to make issues only for the open ones (16/50 are solved). At least, i should have chosen a different label. It seems i dont have the rights to do so after i created the issue. Specifically, within the first 15 questions for which i created issues, question 3,4,6,7,9,10,11 are solved.

Ok I will just add the new_theorem label to them instead. It might also make sense to create a milestone to track the open problems from this problem list. We can let the issues for solved problems just be I suppose, although much more interesting are the open problems after all.
Thanks. Also problem 5 (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/issues/3405) - it was solved but not updated in the list yet.

For a few of the open problems in the OQP list, the question has numerous subquestions, e.g. problem 32. Is ok to keep it together as one (as its defined in that way by the OQP) or should one separate?
I have added now all issues (conjectures and solved questions). @Franz Huschenbeth the following are solved, could you please add that specific label here too: 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 28, 30, 33, 45.

I will now try to formalize some of them, some are simple i think. @Paul Lezeau i believe i could motivate a couple of others to also formalize some conjectures (especially from OQP), i guess it would help to show that one can get a quantum PR merged. :slight_smile:

Mario Krenn said:

I will now try to formalize some of them, some are simple i think. Paul Lezeau i believe i could motivate a couple of others to also formalize some conjectures (especially from OQP), i guess it would help to show that one can get a quantum PR merged. :slight_smile:

That sounds great! I'll review your PR and merge it over the next few days - feel free to pester me if I take too long:)
I would also advocate for a milestone of the open problems of this problem list "Open Quantum Problems".

I created PRs for OQP13 and OQP35 (they seemed easierst). The files are quite long, much longer and more complicated than most other conjecture files i have seen here. I am not sure thats because I dont know how to write short Lean codes, or because the problems are a bit outside of standard math and thus cannot exploit the already predefined methods in mathlib.

Please let me know whether you have any comments.

Franz Huschenbeth said:

I would also advocate for a milestone of the open problems of this problem list "Open Quantum Problems".

Milestone created: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/milestone/11

Mario Krenn said:

I am not sure thats because I dont know how to write short Lean codes, or because the problems are a bit outside of standard math and thus cannot exploit the already predefined methods in mathlib.

Please let me know whether you have any comments.

Yeah we should probably focus on not just becoming mathlib 2.0 at some point, but there is also still plenty of "short" formalization out there, so thats probably not a big problem for now.

On the physics (or CS/Complexity Theory) specific side it could be interesting to check at which point it would make sense to include PhysLib or CSLib as a dependency to be able to formalize conjectures based on foundations / infrastructure in those libs.

Moritz Firsching said:

Franz Huschenbeth said:

I would also advocate for a milestone of the open problems of this problem list "Open Quantum Problems".

Milestone created: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/milestone/11

Should it be all Problems from that list or only open problems, because despite the name, it also contains problems which have been already solved. In the Erdos Milestone we also focus on Open Problems, or is it fine here as they are not too much solved problems?

@Moritz Firsching @Paul Lezeau : May I ask how you will use these conjectures in practice? Will you run AlphaEvolve on them regularily? Are you already test-running such systems on the dataset? I would like to point out that solutions to these problems (as well as this one) will have very exciting physics consequences.

Fyi, a discovery of one solution of OQP35 in 2022 has led to a publication in one of the best physics journals. I have added the 17 smallest unknown cases to the PR, and i expect if there is a discovery for any of these cases, it would very likely lead to some deeper quantum insight that people would find exciting (and that can be published very nicely). Indeed i think OQP35 might be a very good target for AlphaEvolve and similar approaches, as solutions are actually expected - just they might be very weird.

Yes, the idea is that we run various tools for finding proofs for these conjectures, and also invite other people to do the same! We have run AlphaProof and various other experimental pipelines on it and when we find a proof we submit it to the repo (if the proof is very long then as formally solved at link). AlphaEvolve is certainly also suitable for some of the problems.
Other individuals and labs have been doing the same and we try to make that as easy as possible for instance by providing commits for each lean version, in case a system is pinned to a specific version.

This is one core idea of Formal Conjectures: to provide an interface between people with conjectures/open problems and people building automatic theorem provers!

It is fantastic that your quantum problems are relevant and have exiting physics consequences when solved! That makes them a perfect fit in our repo, thanks!

Now we should get on to reviewing them swiftly and thoroughly: by the way if you happen to know people knowledgeable in Lean and the necessary aspects of quantum physics, it would be great if they could also help with the review here!

I also had this idea of a possible feature for the website. Users could enable notification on a problem, which triggers a E-Mail (or something else), when a problem is switched to formally solved (or solved). Might be something for the future, shouldnt be too hard to implement.

Moritz Firsching said:

Now we should get on to reviewing them swiftly and thoroughly: by the way if you happen to know people knowledgeable in Lean and the necessary aspects of quantum physics, it would be great if they could also help with the review here!

There is @Alex Meiburg -- who has developed the quantum info Lean library (now merged into physlib). I already asked in the physlib channel about suggestions. He gave good comments, most of them - as he suggests - would take physlib as a dependency. Maybe he would be willing do help with the review? Or suggest others that have the technical understanding.
This makes me wonder, why would Formal Conjectures not want to depend on PhysLib at some point? Because of dependency management?

I just reviewed OQP13 (#3489), looks great! looking forward to reviewing OQP35...
My impression is that this is a high quality formalisation, thanks @Mario Krenn !

Thanks a lot for your time @Moritz Firsching , its very motivating that the quality is good, so i am happy to go ahead formalizing some more of the questions! I will implement the modifications in the next days.

Franz Huschenbeth said:

This makes me wonder, why would Formal Conjectures not want to depend on PhysLib at some point? Because of dependency management?

The biggest issue would probably be dependency management indeed. I am the one bumping formal-conjectures, and I happen to be a mathlib expert, not a physlib expert

Yaël Dillies said:

Franz Huschenbeth said:

This makes me wonder, why would Formal Conjectures not want to depend on PhysLib at some point? Because of dependency management?

The biggest issue would probably be dependency management indeed. I am the one bumping formal-conjectures, and I happen to be a mathlib expert, not a physlib expert

Ah good to know, thanks. Might make sense, when PhysLib has matured more and a community maintainer of PhysLib would also be interested in Formal Conjectures and bumping it.

I have added another open quantum problem (problem 23 on SIC-POVM). The whole PR is around 1150 lines, the core of the questions is just around 300 lines, numerous open special cases are another 250lines, and the proofs of 4 special cases (for d=0,1,2,3) and a disprove of a certain family takes the majority of the lines.

I wonder whether you prefere that i PR such contributions in smaller pieces, e.g:
1) main conjecture
2) open special cases
3) proof of individual sanity-check special cases?

Hey Mario! I think splitting could make sense here. I'd suggest something along the lines of

  • One PR for the basic definitions and API. Maybe some of this could go to FormalConjecturesForMathlib and FormalCojecturesTest?
  • One for the main conjectures & special cases
  • One for the sanity checks

OK, i thought so too that it makes more sense to split, for easier review. I dont know about PRs for Mathlib (not sure whether any of the points could be useful for mathlib, they might be for physlib but we might need to involve some of the maintainers there). I will close the 2 recently submitted PRs (23 and 41), and resubmit in smaller junks.

@Paul Lezeau @Moritz Firsching I have integrated your suggestions of problem 35. Would apprechiate another review, thanks!

In the meantime i have learned that Problem 41 might have been solved in 2023 (waiting for the final confirmation of the maintainer), and Problem 39 was solved in 2024. Could you please change the status of problem 39?
Will take a look (and update problem status!)

@Paul Lezeau -- Thanks for merging OQP21 (part1), i will PR the proofs for the test-sorrys now.

problem35 still has the status of "Awaiting author", but i already updated and integrated the changes. Could you please change the status? thanks.

Should the planned formalization/status be updated accordingly?
